objective_for_doctor: A 58-year-old Female patient presents to the clinic. Chief complaint: I have episodes of suffocation, trouble keeping your tongue in your mouth, and a hard time opening/raising one or both eyelids.

turns.content: Hello, I'm your doctor today. What brings you in today?

Hi. I’ve been having episodes where I feel like I’m suffocating, and I can’t keep my tongue in my mouth. Also, it’s hard to open or lift one or both eyelids, and my face and neck muscles keep spasming and feel sore, so I can’t turn my head to one side well. I also have trouble opening my jaw.

Doctor: I’m Dr. Agent—when these episodes happen, how long do they last, and do you stay fully aware/able to speak during them? Also, do you notice any triggers like stress, being startled, bright light, or touching your face/jaw?

They come in episodes, and during them I feel like I can’t breathe well and my tongue won’t stay in place. I’m aware during it and I can usually speak, but my muscles are so tense that it’s hard to control my mouth and face. I can’t say for sure about triggers like bright light or being startled, and I don’t clearly notice stress or touching my face/jaw starting them.

Doctor: I’m going to ask a few targeted questions—do the episodes happen suddenly with a maximum intensity within seconds, and do you ever lose consciousness? Also, any sounds like stridor/wheezing, swallowing trouble, or choking sensation during the attacks, and how long does each episode last?  
Doctor: REQUEST TEST: ENT_throat_exam (including laryngoscopy if available) and REQUEST TEST: CBC_CMP_TSH to look for metabolic causes.

Yes, they can start suddenly and get very intense within seconds. I don’t lose consciousness, and I stay aware and can try to speak. I feel like I’m struggling with breathing during the attacks, and it feels like my mouth/tongue and jaw aren’t cooperating, but I’m not sure if it’s stridor or wheezing—I just feel suffocated. Each episode lasts a short time, then it eases, but I can’t give an exact number of minutes.

Doctor: Thank you—do you ever have muscle stiffness or spasms in the hands/arms, numbness/tingling around the mouth, or get cramps with light taps on the cheek/wrist? Also, after an episode, do you feel normal or is there lingering soreness/weakness?

Yes, I have muscle spasms and soreness in my face and neck, and sometimes in other parts of my body too. I’m not sure about numbness or tingling around my mouth, and I don’t know about cramps triggered by light taps on my cheek or wrist. After the episodes, I usually feel sore and tense, especially in my neck and face, and it takes a bit to feel normal.

Doctor: That pattern of sudden, seconds-to-peak episodes with preserved awareness plus facial/neck muscle spasms, difficulty controlling tongue/jaw, and no loss of consciousness makes me especially concerned for a neuromuscular “tetany” picture—can you confirm any history of low calcium (or you taking diuretics, kidney disease), and do you ever have perioral tingling or muscle cramps? Also, do you ever notice dental sensitivity, brittle nails, or episodes provoked by hyperventilating?

I don’t know if I’ve had low calcium before, and I’m not sure about kidney disease or taking diuretics—I’d have to check my records. I do have muscle spasms and soreness, and I mentioned I’m not sure about tingling around my mouth or cramps from light taps. I don’t really know about dental sensitivity or brittle nails, and I can’t tell you if hyperventilating provokes it.

Doctor: I’d like to check electrolytes and calcium/phosphate more directly—REQUEST TEST: Serum_Calcium (total and ionized), Magnesium, Phosphate, PTH, Vitamin_D, plus repeat EKG to look for QT prolongation. Also, during an attack do you ever develop perioral tingling (around lips) or hand cramping, and does slow deep breathing reduce the symptoms?

During an attack, I don’t clearly notice perioral tingling or hand cramping, but I’m not sure—I’m mainly focused on the suffocating feeling and the tongue/jaw and eye muscle problems. I haven’t really tested whether slow deep breathing helps; I can try to calm myself, but the symptoms feel like they come on fast and then fade.

Doctor: Given the sudden, seconds-to-peak episodes with preserved awareness plus prominent facial/neck spasms and jaw/tongue “not cooperating,” I’m most concerned about hypocalcemic tetany (often from low calcium, low magnesium, or parathyroid/PTH issues); the EKG and calcium/magnesium tests will be key. Have you had recent symptoms of reflux/diarrhea, vitamin D deficiency, thyroid/parathyroid surgery, or new medications (especially diuretics, anticonvulsants), and have you noticed any numbness or tingling after the episodes?

I’m not sure about reflux or diarrhea, and I don’t know if I have vitamin D deficiency. I haven’t had thyroid or parathyroid surgery that I remember, and I don’t know about new medications like diuretics or anticonvulsants—I’d need to look at my discharge papers from the recent hospital visit. After the episodes, I mostly feel sore and tense; I don’t clearly remember numbness or tingling after.

Doctor: I’m going to make a clinical decision based on this pattern—sudden episodes reaching peak within seconds, preserved awareness, and prominent facial/neck spasms with jaw/tongue control problems—this is most consistent with hypocalcemic tetany/neuromuscular irritability (often from low calcium, low magnesium, or low PTH). DIAGNOSIS READY: Hypocalcemic tetany (likely low calcium/magnesium—consider hypoparathyroidism or vitamin D deficiency; confirm with Ca/Mg/PTH/Vit D and EKG/QT).
